title: MemCast: Memory-Driven Time Series Forecasting with Experience-Conditioned Reasoning
one_liner: A time series forecaster that learns from past attempts and stores lessons as memory guides to improve future predictions.
lead: Large language models can now predict what happens next in a sequence of numbers (stock prices, sensor readings, weather patterns). But they start from scratch each time: no memory of what worked before, no lessons from past failures. MemCast changes this by storing experiences as structured memory — historical patterns that guided past successes, reasoning wisdom from how the model explored different ideas, and general laws learned from the data — then using that memory to guide new forecasts.

paras: A time series is a sequence of numbers over time: daily stock prices, hourly temperatures, minute-by-minute traffic counts. Predicting the next value in that sequence is hard because past patterns matter. Large language models are good at pattern recognition, so they can be trained to do this forecasting.

But today's LLM-based forecasters do not store lessons from their mistakes. When asked to forecast a new sequence, a model starts with no memory of what worked on similar sequences before. If it tried to predict a holiday spike and failed on one sequence, it repeats the same failed reasoning on the next holiday spike. The model has no systematic way to learn from its own experience across many forecasts.

callout.html: MemCast organizes forecasting experience into memory — patterns from past successes, reasoning steps that worked, and general rules extracted from data — and uses this memory to guide future predictions.

steps.b: Step 1: Learn experience from training data
steps.text: Train the model on past sequences, capturing outcomes, reasoning steps, and feature patterns.
Build hierarchical storage: historical patterns (outcomes that happened), reasoning wisdom (good reasoning paths), general laws (rules that held across data).

steps.b: Step 3: Guide new predictions with patterns
steps.text: When forecasting a new sequence, retrieve similar historical patterns and use them to steer the model's initial reasoning.

steps.b: Step 4: Refine with wisdom and laws
steps.text: Use reasoning wisdom to pick better exploration paths, because stored steps that worked before are more likely to lead to good forecasts than random tries. Use general laws as sanity checks and iterate to stay consistent, because forecasts violating known rules are wrong by definition.
Update confidence in each memory entry based on new forecasts, but never let the model see the actual answer on test data.

object.h2: What the paper changes: memory state
paras: MemCast adds a new object to forecasting: structured memory. Before, the model only had its learned weights (the parameters trained once on the training set). Now, MemCast introduces a second learnable object — a hierarchical memory bank that grows and adapts as the model forecasts.

hidden.name: Memory entry confidence (how much to trust each stored lesson)
paras: As the model forecasts on new sequences, it learns whether each stored lesson is actually useful. A confidence score (a number from low to high) for each memory entry tells the model how much to trust that pattern or rule.

MemCast measures confidence by tracking: when a memory entry is retrieved, does the forecast succeed or fail? If retrieved patterns led to good forecasts, confidence increases. If they led to errors, confidence decreases. The paper's key challenge is updating these scores without accidentally learning from the test set itself — the trick is to only update based on patterns the model itself generated, not from seeing the correct answer.

heat.caption: Darker means higher confidence. Darker entries guide more forecasts; lighter entries are being phased out as unreliable.

reads.html: Confidence is how much the model trusts a memory entry — the higher the confidence, the more the model listens to that stored lesson.
Dynamic confidence adaptation: a learned scoring mechanism that updates each memory entry's confidence based on forecast outcomes, constrained so it never sees the ground truth.

mechanism.h2: Why storing and refining memory helps
paras: The mechanism is a learning loop. A standard forecaster trains once, then predicts the same way forever — it cannot improve from experience. MemCast breaks this by making experience learnable.

When the model forecasts on a new sequence, three things happen in order: First, it retrieves similar patterns from memory and uses them to guide which reasoning path to explore (this avoids re-exploring dead ends). Second, it uses stored reasoning wisdom — the steps that worked before — to steer how it explores. Third, after proposing a forecast, it checks that proposal against stored general laws; if it violates a rule, the model re-thinks and tries again. Each time this works, the confidence in that memory entry goes up. Each time it fails, confidence goes down. Over many forecasts, memory entries become increasingly tuned to what actually helps because the model reinforces entries that lead to success and suppresses ones that lead to failure — a form of learning that never stops, even during deployment.

Why does this work? Because patterns that kept failing in training never built high confidence; they stay dormant. Patterns that consistently led to correct predictions accumulate high confidence and guide more future forecasts. The hierarchical structure has three levels: specific patterns stored from past sequences, reasoning wisdom that captures good exploration strategies, and general laws that hold broadly across the data. This layering means the model has both concrete lessons from similar past sequences and abstract rules to fall back on.

stages.s: Use patterns to guide reasoning path selection
Check reasoning steps against stored wisdom
Update confidence in memory entries based on result

math.words: New confidence equals old confidence plus a small adjustment based on how well this forecasting step matched the memory entry's advice.
symbols: confidence value for memory entry m after this forecast
how much each forecast result shifts confidence (a small number, like 0.01)
how well the memory entry matched what the model actually did (1 if it matched, 0 if it did not match, between 0 and 1 if it partially matched)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario: Pattern_1 stored a rule about holiday spikes. On a new forecast with a holiday, the model uses Pattern_1 to guide reasoning.
Match score: Does the forecast match what Pattern_1 predicted? Yes, fully. match_score = 1.0
If instead the forecast had disagreed with Pattern_1, match_score = 0 and confidence_new = 0.60 + 0.05 * 0 = 0.60 (no change)

math.note: Each memory entry's confidence grows when it guides successful forecasts, because the model tracks whether reasoning steps it used actually matched what it decided to forecast, and shrinks when it leads to errors, using the same internal matching signal. This works without ever seeing the ground truth because the update only looks at the model's own choices, not at correct answers.

charts.title: Standard LLM-based forecaster (no memory)
charts.note: Same model every time. Performance gradually drifts downward as the model encounters unfamiliar patterns.

charts.title: MemCast (memory-based forecaster)
charts.note: Memory improves over time because lessons from early sequences accumulate into higher confidence, and later forecasts consult that accumulated memory, so they inherit the guidance of earlier successes without re-learning from scratch.

items.b: Memory contamination: updating confidence using ground truth
items.html: If the model peeks at the actual next value (the ground truth), it can game its confidence scores to match any data. The paper's fix: only update based on reasoning steps the model generates, not from seeing the correct answer. This is the core constraint of dynamic confidence adaptation.

items.b: Noisy memory: storing failed patterns at high confidence
items.html: Early forecasts might build wrong patterns that seem to work by luck. If confidence updates too aggressively, these bad patterns stick around and mislead later forecasts. The fix is a slow learning rate (alpha stays small) so confidence changes gradually.

items.b: Catastrophic forgetting: adapting memory breaks old lessons
items.html: If confidence updates too freely, high-confidence entries might suddenly flip based on one bad forecast from a very different sequence type. The hierarchical structure mitigates this because specific patterns adapt quickly (they apply only to similar sequences, so one mismatch is expected noise) while general laws adapt slowly (they apply everywhere, so they need many mismatches to flip), so abstract lessons persist even when specific patterns are wrong.

Organizing memory into patterns (specific outcomes), wisdom (reasoning strategies), and laws (general rules) creates natural resistance to noise. Specific lessons can adapt quickly; abstract rules resist one-off noise and stay stable. Confidence updates only from internally-generated reasoning steps, never from seeing answers.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple forecaster on a small time series dataset (e.g., a toy monthly sales sequence with seasonal spikes). First, train a baseline LLM-based forecaster on the first 60 percent of the data. Then, without retraining, deploy it on the remaining 40 percent while MemCast's memory adapts. Track the forecast error for each new sequence. Measure how much memory-guided forecasts improve over the purely-trained baseline, because accumulated memory allows later forecasts to benefit from what earlier ones learned.
demo.metric_eq: Improvement = (error_baseline - error_memcast) / error_baseline, measured as the average across all test sequences
demo.closing: The demo must show that memory improves forecasts on sequences the model never saw in training because patterns that predicted well accumulate high confidence while ones that fail drop in confidence, and the high-confidence patterns guide new forecasts to better answers.
